title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis & Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State: Recognition, Fluids, Potassium and Safe Resolution
html:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) are life-threatening metabolic emergencies. Both cause dehydration and electrolyte losses, but DKA features clinically important ketone production and acidosis, whereas HHS features profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with little or no major ketoacidosis. Mixed presentations occur. The RN assesses circulation and mentation, supports ordered fluid and insulin therapy, watches potassium and osmolality trends, and does not declare recovery merely because glucose has fallen.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate the dominant clinical and laboratory patterns of DKA, HHS, and mixed crisis.
  • Recognize euglycemic DKA, including presentations associated with SGLT2 inhibitors.
  • Prioritize volume and perfusion assessment, potassium safety, insulin delivery, and close reassessment.
  • Explain why dextrose may be added while insulin continues during DKA recovery.
  • Monitor for hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, fluid overload, and rapid osmotic change.
  • Plan a safe transition to subcutaneous insulin and prevention before discharge.

Why the crises differ

In DKA, insufficient effective insulin permits lipolysis and ketone formation. Ketones cause metabolic acidosis; osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia produces water and electrolyte deficits. Symptoms may include thirst, polyuria, abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, dehydration, deep or rapid breathing, fruity breath, weakness, and altered mentation. DKA can occur in type 1 or type 2 diabetes and at glucose levels that are not dramatically high, especially with SGLT2 inhibitor exposure, pregnancy, or reduced food intake.

In HHS, enough insulin usually remains to limit major ketone formation but not to control severe hyperglycemia. Prolonged osmotic diuresis leads to marked water deficit and hyperosmolality; neurologic changes can be prominent, from lethargy and confusion to seizure or coma. The two syndromes overlap, so evaluate ketones, acid–base status, glucose, and osmolality rather than labeling a client by diabetes type or glucose alone.

Do not let a glucose number hide the crisis
A person with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, and significant ketones may have DKA even when glucose is only modestly elevated. HHS can also be life-threatening without marked acidosis.

Build a complete initial picture

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs, mental status, hydration, mucous membranes, capillary refill, weight when available, urine output, and signs of infection or another trigger. Ask about insulin omission or pump failure, illness, myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis, steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, and access to food, medication, and supplies. Obtain ordered point-of-care glucose, blood beta-hydroxybutyrate when available, venous or arterial pH and bicarbonate, electrolytes including potassium, sodium and kidney function, and measured or calculated osmolality when HHS is suspected. Other testing follows the clinical trigger.

Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is useful for DKA diagnosis and resolution; urine ketones can lag or appear to worsen during recovery as ketone species shift. Corrected sodium and effective osmolality help interpret water balance and neurologic risk. A normal-looking serum potassium at presentation does not mean total-body potassium stores are adequate: urinary losses can be large while insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells.

Restore perfusion without causing overload

Ordered isotonic or balanced crystalloid fluids treat circulatory depletion and improve renal perfusion. Determine the initial urgency from blood pressure, pulse, perfusion, mentation, urine output, and the degree of dehydration. Reassess response frequently. Older adults and people with heart failure, kidney failure, or other risk of overload need particularly careful fluid selection and rate; crackles, increasing oxygen requirement, edema, or worsening work of breathing may signal harm. Do not apply one fixed volume or rate to every client.

In HHS, severe hyperosmolality often developed over days, so an overly rapid fall in glucose or osmolality may create neurologic risk. Follow the ordered monitoring and correction plan. Observe mental status closely, and report new headache, seizure, focal deficit, or falling consciousness rather than assuming it is expected fatigue.

Potassium safety comes before insulin speed

Insulin drives potassium into cells; fluids and correction of acidosis can further lower serum potassium. Review the current potassium result, rhythm, kidney function, and urine output before and during treatment. A low potassium level can cause dangerous dysrhythmia and respiratory-muscle weakness. In the adult consensus pathway, when potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L, potassium replacement is initiated and insulin is delayed until potassium is corrected above that threshold under an authorized protocol. Recheck frequently because potassium may fall quickly after insulin starts. Never add potassium without checking the current order, concentration, route, renal function, and monitoring requirements.

Hyperkalemia may also be present initially, especially with kidney dysfunction. Assess the ECG and treat an unstable rhythm under the emergency pathway; do not assume insulin alone has resolved the total potassium problem. Trend magnesium, phosphate, acid–base status, and kidney function as ordered. Routine bicarbonate is not a standard substitute for fluids and insulin; special circumstances require physician-directed assessment.

Insulin resolves ketogenesis; glucose decline is only one marker

Follow the prescribed insulin route and rate. Intravenous insulin is commonly used for severe DKA or HHS in monitored settings; selected mild uncomplicated DKA may follow a different supervised protocol. Verify the pump, concentration, line, ordered glucose checks, and transition plan. As glucose falls in DKA, dextrose may be added to fluids so insulin can continue suppressing ketone production until acidosis and ketonemia resolve. Stopping insulin solely because glucose reached a near-normal value can allow ketoacidosis to recur.

Watch for hypoglycemia and respond according to protocol. In HHS, monitor glucose and osmolality changes together, as well as hemodynamics and neurologic status. Do not equate a single improved glucose value with clinical recovery. The team determines resolution using the syndrome-specific laboratory and clinical criteria, including ketone and acid–base recovery for DKA or osmolality and mental-status recovery for HHS.

Find and treat the precipitating cause

Common triggers include infection, missed insulin, device malfunction, new diabetes, ischemic events, medications, dehydration, and barriers to care. Obtain ordered cultures and give prescribed antimicrobials when infection is suspected without delaying urgent stabilization. Check the insulin delivery system and reconcile recent medicines. Avoid framing omission as nonadherence before asking about affordability, health literacy, transport, illness, nausea, or inability to obtain supplies. A crisis often reflects a system or access problem that needs a durable solution.

Transition safely after stabilization

When the client is clinically ready to eat and the crisis has resolved, coordinate the ordered transition from IV to subcutaneous insulin with an appropriate overlap to prevent a gap in insulin effect. Verify type 1 basal-insulin continuity, ability to eat, kidney function, medication changes, and monitoring frequency. At discharge, use teach-back for glucose and ketone monitoring, insulin or other medicine use, sick-day actions, hydration and food plan, when to call or seek emergency care, access to supplies, and follow-up. A previous crisis increases future risk, so prevention education is part of treatment.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Assess mentation, perfusion, breathing, vomiting, urine output, glucose, ketones, pH or bicarbonate, potassium, sodium, osmolality, kidney function, medications, and triggers.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish DKA, HHS, mixed crisis, and euglycemic DKA; understand that serum potassium can be misleading despite a total-body deficit.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Shock, severe hypokalemia or dysrhythmia, altered airway protection, cerebral deterioration, and fluid-overload risk require immediate attention.
  4. Generate solutions: Support ABCs and perfusion, follow ordered fluids and potassium correction, verify insulin safety, add dextrose when indicated while ketones clear, and identify the precipitating problem.
  5. Take action: Use frequent protocol-driven glucose, electrolyte, ketone, acid–base, fluid, and neurologic checks; report deviations promptly and avoid independent rate or dose changes.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm improvement in perfusion, hydration, mentation, potassium and osmolality, and DKA ketone and acidosis resolution—not glucose alone—before transition and discharge teaching.

Clinical example

A person with type 1 diabetes and several days of vomiting arrives dehydrated, tachycardic, deeply breathing, and confused. Glucose is elevated, blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is high, bicarbonate is low, and potassium is 3.2 mmol/L. The RN recognizes DKA with high risk of treatment-induced hypokalemia, calls for urgent monitored care, supports prescribed fluids, confirms ECG and electrolyte monitoring, and escalates the need for potassium correction before insulin under the adult protocol. The RN continues to trend ketones and acid–base status after glucose falls and helps identify why insulin delivery was interrupted before discharge.

Original educational synthesis. DKA and HHS diagnosis, fluids, potassium replacement, insulin delivery, dextrose addition, correction rates, resolution criteria, and transition require current client data, authorized orders, local emergency protocols, frequent laboratory reassessment, and qualified supervision.
